"On an analysis of the aforesaid judgments from various High Courts, we find that the High Courts of Andhra Pradesh, Bombay, Delhi, Gauhati, Himachal Pradesh,
Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh, are right in holding that if Domestic Incident Report has been received by the Magistrate either from the Protection Officer or the service provider then it becomes obligatory on the part of the Magistrate to Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT take note of the said report before passing an order on the application filed by the aggrieved party, but if no complaint or application of domestic violence is received by the Magistrate from the Protection Officer or the service provider, the question of considering such a report does not arise at all.

sentences.text: As already discussed, the D.V.Act does not make it mandatory for an aggrieved person to make an application before a Magistrate only through the Protection Officer or a service provider.
An aggrieved person can directly make an application to the jurisdictional Magistrate by herself or by engaging the services of an Advocate.
In such a case, the filing of a Domestic Incident Report by a Protection Officer or service provider does not arise.
In such circumstances, it cannot be held that the Magistrate is not empowered to make any order interim or final, under the provisions of the D.V.Act, granting reliefs to the aggrieved persons.

The Magistrate can take cognizance of the complaint or application filed by the aggrieved person and issue notice to the respondent under Section 12 of the D.V. Act even in the absence of Domestic Incident Report under Rule 5.

Thus, the Magistrate has jurisdiction to take cognizance of the complaint under Section 12 of the D.V. Act in the absence of a Domestic Incident Report under Rule 5 when the complaint is not filed Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT on behalf of the aggrieved person through a Protection Officer or service provider.

Such a purposeful interpretation has to be given bearing in mind the fact that the immediate relief would have to be given to an aggrieved person and hence the proviso cannot be interpreted in a manner which would be contrary to the object of the D.V.Act which renders Section 12 bereft of its object and purpose".
5.

This Court has gone through the above cited principle, wherein it was observed that Section 12 of the PWDV Act, 2005 does not mandate a magistrate to consider the Domestic Incident Report (DIR) filed by the protection officer or service provider before issuing any orders under the Act.

It was also clarified that, even in the absence of a DIR, the magistrate is empowered to proceed ex Asha Rani vs Karthik R on 10 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65709175/
2 parte and issue interim as well as final orders under the provisions of the Act.

sentences.text: To establish that the petitioner was aware of his first marriage, the respondent suggested during her cross- examination that he was not present during the marriage proposal.
The petitioner admitted this, stating she only spoke to the respondent over the phone and was informed he was working in Chennai at the time.
She further acknowledged that she did not meet the respondent before their marriage proposal and did not inquire whether he agreed to the marriage.
Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT 20.
However, she admitted that the marriage arrangements were made in the presence of the respondent's uncle, aunt, grandparents, and friends, despite the respondent not being physically present.
She also admitted with the suggestion that the respondent was absent during these arrangements.
Apart from these points, no evidence has been presented to prove that the petitioner knew about the respondent's alleged first marriage.
21. Therefore, the respondent failed to prove that the petitioner was aware of his previous marriage.
Even if it is assumed that the petitioner knew about the respondent's imprisonment, the respondent did not provide evidence to demonstrate that she also knew about his first marriage.
As a result, the respondent's claim remains unsubstantiated.

In essence, despite efforts to establish otherwise during cross- examination, the respondent's case lacked the necessary evidence to support his assertion that the petitioner was aware of his first marriage.
This critical lack of proof weakened his Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT argument and left his claim unsubstantiated in the eyes of the court.
22. During the cross-examination of RW.1, the respondent himself admitted that his date of birth is 21.03.1991.
According to his own testimony, he married Sruthi on 16.05.2009.
Additionally, he acknowledged the existence of a letter confronted to him during cross-examination, marked as Ex.P.33, wherein his date of birth is recorded as 21.03.1991.
23. Under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, one of the essential conditions for a valid marriage is that the groom must have attained the age of 21 years at the time of marriage.
This requirement is intended to ensure that both parties to the marriage are legally competent and capable of entering into a marital union.
24. In the present case, it has been established through the respondent's own admission during cross-examination that his date of birth is 21.03.1991.
Furthermore, he confirmed that Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT he married Sruthi on 16.05.2009.
This timeline indicates that on the date of his marriage, 16.05.2009, the respondent was approximately 18 years and 2 months old.
The discrepancy between the respondent's age at the time of marriage and the minimum age requirement stipulated under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act raises a significant legal issue.
According to the Act, a groom must have completed 21 years of age to be eligible for marriage.
Since the respondent was under 21 years old when he married Sruthi, his marriage could potentially be considered void under the law.

sentences.text: In addition to that the respondent, in attempting to assert that his marriage with the petitioner was due to coercion or threat, faces a significant challenge in explaining why he did not seek annulment of the marriage through the appropriate legal channels.
If the respondent contends that his marriage with the petitioner occurred under coercion or threat, it would typically imply that he was forced into the marriage against his will or under duress.
In such cases, the law provides recourse for annulment of the marriage through legal processes aimed at Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT addressing marriages entered into without free consent.
The absence of any action by the respondent to seek annulment raises questions about the validity of his claim.
If he genuinely believed that the marriage was coerced or induced under threat, he would be expected to approach the appropriate legal forum to have the marriage declared null and void.
This legal course of action is provided under various provisions of family law, including those that address marriages entered into under duress or coercion.

By failing to explain why he did not pursue annulment proceedings despite alleging coercion or threat, the respondent's argument regarding the circumstances of the marriage lacks a crucial legal basis.
26. During his cross-examination, the respondent admitted that he married the petitioner according to Hindu customs and did not file any case for the annulment of their marriage.
Furthermore, he admitted that he did not initiate any legal proceedings to validate his marriage with Sruthi.

The admission by the respondent that he married the petitioner according to Hindu customs indicates his acceptance of the Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT marriage ceremony conducted as per traditional Hindu rites.
This acknowledgment implies that, despite any alleged coercion or threat he may claim, he participated willingly in the marriage ceremony with the petitioner.

27. Moreover, the respondent's statement that he did not file any case for the annulment of his marriage with the petitioner raises questions regarding the validity of his claim of coercion or threat.

If the respondent genuinely believed that his marriage with the petitioner was coerced or conducted under duress, he could have sought legal recourse to annul the marriage through appropriate legal channels.
The absence of any such legal action suggests a lack of substantiation for his claim of coercion.
Additionally, the respondent's admission that he did not initiate any legal proceedings to validate his marriage with Sruthi further complicates his position.
If he intended to establish the legitimacy of his marriage with Sruthi, he would typically need to pursue legal validation through court proceedings.
The failure to take such action undermines his Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT argument regarding the circumstances of his marriages and may impact the credibility of his testimony.

28. Therefore, based on the respondent's admissions and the observations made in the present petition, the petitioner has successfully proven that her marriage with the respondent occurred in accordance with Hindu customs.
At this stage, the burden shifts to the respondent to prove that he was previously married to someone else and that the petitioner knew about this fact before marrying him.
However, there is no material available on record to discharge this burden.
As a result, the respondent fails to prove that the petitioner was aware of his alleged first marriage or that Sruthi is his legally wedded wife.
The respondent himself admitted to his marriage with the petitioner and stated that he had no relationship with her after just 5 days of marriage, as he left to live with Sruthi.

sentences.text: This Court has carefully perused the legal principles cited above, wherein the Hon'ble High Court of Patna addressed situation involving women who had obtained divorce from her husband and subsequently sought protection under the PWDV Act due to alleged domestic violence during her marriage.
It was observed that divorced women may not maintain a petition under the provisions of the PWDV Act.
Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT 31.

The Hon'ble High Court of Himachal Pradesh held that in the absence of evidence of maltreatment or violence and considering the dissolution of the marriage, the appellate court erred in awarding maintenance to the complainant, a decision that was rightly reversed by the trial court.
This Court acknowledges and respects the principles established by the Hon'ble High Courts in those decisions.

32. However, in the present case, it is undisputed that at the time the petitioner filed her petition,
she had not yet divorced the respondent.
Subsequently, she remarried and had a child from that marriage.
Therefore, the factual circumstances of the present case differ from those in the decisions cited by the respondent's counsel.
Thus, the principles laid down in the aforementioned decisions are not directly applicable to the present case at hand.

The petitioner's eligibility to seek relief under the PWDV Act should be considered based on her marital status at the time of filing the petition and the specific circumstances surrounding her situation.

The Court emphasizes that the petitioner's rights Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT under the PWDV Act should be evaluated based on the legal status that existed when she initiated legal proceedings, ensuring that her access to remedies under domestic violence laws is appropriately determined in light of her circumstances.
33. In the context of marital relationships, emotional abuse is recognized as a form of domestic violence under Section 3 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence (PWDV) Act.

sentences.text: This section defines emotional abuse broadly to include any act, omission, or conduct that causes mental or emotional harm to the aggrieved person.

Importantly, emotional abuse does not always involve physical violence but can profoundly affect a person's psychological well-being and overall quality of Asha Rani vs Karthik R on 10 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65709175/

Therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that, the petitioner has proved that, petitioner has been subjected to cruelty and domestic violence by the respondent and the respondent has deserted and neglected the petitioner without Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT providing any maintenance.
With these observations, this Court answers the points No.1 and 2 in the AFFIRMATIVE.
34. Point No.3 :
As discussed above petitioner has proved that, petitioner has been subjected to cruelty and deserted by the respondent.
The petitioner has asserted that the respondent failed to provide maintenance or arrange for residence.
It is further contended that the respondent has a presence in the film industry, with the respondent's family also engaged in film production and earning rental income from immovable properties.

It is asserted that the respondent is actively involved in financial activities, including a money lending business under the name of M/s. Sri Ranga Finance, as evidenced by Ex. P.14, a valid money lending license issued by the relevant regulatory authority.

35. Moreover, the petitioner has brought forward a series of electricity bills (Ex. P.4, P.5, P.7 to P.13,
and P.15 to P.21), all registered in the name of Rangaswamy, the respondent's father.

These bills,
which reflect ongoing utility Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT usage, strongly indicate the family's substantial involvement with multiple properties.

Ex. P.22, the Record of Rights of Survey Number 63/1, details the ownership of agricultural land measuring 1 acre 7 guntas in Srigandadakavalu,
Bengaluru North, registered solely in the name of the respondent's father.
This ownership underscores the family's significant holdings in immovable properties.
Furthermore, the respondent's affidavit regarding assets and liabilities claims a monthly income of Rs. 20,000.
However, crucially, the respondent has not provided supporting bank statements to verify this income assertion, raising doubts about the accuracy of his financial disclosure.

36. Upon thorough perusal of the aforementioned documentary evidence, it is abundantly clear that the respondent and his family enjoy substantial income from various sources, including rental income from properties and income generated through business activities.
These resources highlight the respondent's capacity to provide financial support and stable living conditions, which he has allegedly failed to fulfil for the petitioner.

This court is of the opinion that the Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT evidence presented convincingly demonstrates the respondent's financial capability and obligations, reinforcing the petitioner's claims of neglect and abandonment in this matter 37.

The Court has taken note of the fact that despite the petitioner having obtained a divorce from the respondent and subsequently entering into a second marriage, she endured domestic violence during her initial marriage while residing in the shared household with the respondent.
Due to these circumstances, the Court has determined that the petitioner is entitled to receive compensation amounting to Rs. 15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakhs only) from the respondent.
This compensation is seen as an obligatory duty on the part of the respondent, who was formerly married to the petitioner.
This obligation remains irrespective of the dissolution of their previous marriage.

As already discussed, the D.V.Act does not make it mandatory for an aggrieved person to make an application before a Magistrate only through the Protection Officer or a service provider.
An aggrieved person can directly make an application to the jurisdictional Magistrate by herself or by engaging the services of an Advocate.
In such a case, the filing of a Domestic Incident Report by a Protection Officer or service provider does not arise.
In such circumstances, it cannot be held that the Magistrate is not empowered to make any order interim or final, under the provisions of the D.V.Act, granting reliefs to the aggrieved persons.
Such a purposeful interpretation has to be given bearing in mind the fact that the immediate relief would have to be given to an aggrieved person and hence the proviso cannot be interpreted in a manner which would be contrary to the object of the D.V.Act which renders Section 12 bereft of its object and purpose".

23. Under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, one of the essential conditions for a valid marriage is that the groom must have attained the age of 21 years at the time of marriage.
This requirement is intended to ensure that both parties to the marriage are legally competent and capable of entering into a marital union.

The discrepancy between the respondent's age at the time of marriage and the minimum age requirement stipulated under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act raises a significant legal issue.

If the respondent contends that his marriage with the petitioner occurred under coercion or threat, it would typically imply that he was forced into the marriage against his will or under duress.
In such cases, the law provides recourse for annulment of the marriage through legal processes aimed at Crl.Mis.No.159/2013 JUDGMENT addressing marriages entered into without free consent.
The absence of any action by the respondent to seek annulment raises questions about the validity of his claim.
If he genuinely believed that the marriage was coerced or induced under threat, he would be expected to approach the appropriate legal forum to have the marriage declared null and void.
If the respondent genuinely believed that his marriage with the petitioner was coerced or conducted under duress, he could have sought legal recourse to annul the marriage through appropriate legal channels.
